Smallpox in the Americas. Following Columbus's arrival in 1492, a catastrophic wave of epidemics swept the continents. Smallpox, endemic in Eurasia and Africa for millennia, was entirely absent from the Americas. The Indigenous peoples had no acquired immunity to Old World pathogens. Over the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, an estimated 90 percent of the pre-Columbian Indigenous population died from European diseases.

The first documented smallpox outbreak in Hispaniola occurred in 1518 and 1519, killing an estimated 30 to 50 percent of the Taíno population within a few years. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was ravaged by smallpox in 1520 during Cortés's siege. The epidemic killed the Aztec emperor Cuitláhuac and weakened military resistance at the critical moment of European invasion. Scholars estimate that between 56 and 100 million Indigenous people died over 130 years.

Smallpox was not the only killer. Measles, typhus, typhoid, and influenza created waves of repeated epidemics that prevented population recovery. These epidemics were not intentional bioweapons in most cases. Diseases spread unknowingly through trade and military contact, though some Spanish soldiers allegedly used infected blankets against Indigenous peoples in documented instances.

The demographic collapse was accompanied by ecological collapse. Abandoned Indigenous settlements allowed forests to regrow, reshaping the continental environment. Agricultural societies fragmented, fundamentally transforming the landscape that European colonizers encountered. The smallpox pandemic genocide was one of history's largest and most rapid population collapses.
